title: Engle-Granger, step by step — and why its critical values differ

explain.prompt: In 5–7 sentences: describe the two steps of Engle-Granger and its null hypothesis; interpret WTI–Brent; then explain coffee–Brent, where the ADF statistic on the residuals gives a naive p-value of 0.038 but the Engle-Granger p-value is 0.50 — which one is right and why? What does the brent ~ coffee ordering show, and what are the limits of the method?
rubric: Step 1: OLS of y on a constant and x in levels (the candidate long-run relation). Step 2: unit-root test on the residuals. H0: no cointegration (residuals have a unit root); H1: cointegration (residuals stationary).

WTI ~ Brent: β ≈ 0.98, statistic ≈ −7.4 far below the 5 % Engle-Granger critical value (≈ −3.34), p ≈ 0 → cointegrated: an equilibrium WTI keeps returning to, consistent with the arbitrage hypothesis.

Coffee ~ Brent: same statistic for both p-values (−2.05). The naive p-value (0.038) uses Dickey-Fuller tables, valid for an observed series; here β was chosen by OLS to make the residual as small and stationary-looking as possible, so the critical values must be more negative (−3.34 instead of ≈ −1.94). Correct p = 0.50: no cointegration.
The naive reading would 'confirm' a relationship that does not exist — the spurious regression of 4.6 coming back through the back door.
The result depends on which variable is on the left (brent ~ coffee gives p ≈ 0.20); Engle-Granger finds at most one relation, has low power, and is distorted by structural breaks.
Without an economic mechanism (arbitrage for WTI–Brent), even a rejection would be suspect.
